original_summary: Shubik's dollar auction: two players take turns raising a public bid for a $1 prize by a minimum increment. The highest bidder wins the dollar and pays their bid, and the losing bidder also pays their last bid. The game is a classic escalation trap in which sunk costs push both players to bid past the prize's value.

review.evidence: The platform only decides who wins. With two players, the auction winner nets 1 - b and the loser pays b - 0.05. The winner therefore always ends 0.95 ahead, whatever the bid level. Raising is always relatively better than dropping, so 'always raise' cannot lose, the auction never ends rationally, and dropping out always loses.

Under a who-ends-higher rule the outcome is decided by who refuses to stop, or by a tie-breaking cap. Absolute payoffs, where real skill (not entering, or stopping early) lives, are invisible to the winner rule.
It is a single one-shot event with an obvious relative strategy (never yield). There is nothing to improve beyond that.

Information is perfect: the bid and the high bidder are public, and the prize value is common knowledge. The only inference is guessing the opponent's resolve, and the winner rule makes resolve infinite.
Payoffs are pure arithmetic on bids.
Turn-based and text-only, but the alternating open-ended raise loop has no fixed length. That needs unbounded repetition, which the flat step list handles poorly.

problems: In a two-player highest-total game, winning the auction always beats losing it by 0.95 regardless of price, so 'always raise' cannot lose and escalation is unbounded.
Perfect information: there is no hidden state to infer, only an unbounded test of will.
A single one-shot auction gives no planning over several rounds and no budget trade-offs.
The open-ended alternating raise loop has no fixed number of steps, which the flat step list cannot build cleanly.
Skill at the game, knowing when to stay out or stop, is not rewarded by a who-ends-higher rule with two players.

changes.what: Three or four players instead of two.
changes.why: Two bidders locked in an escalation war both bleed coins while a bystander who stayed out pulls ahead. Escalation becomes genuinely costly under a highest-total rule, which restores the trap's meaning.
changes.fixes: In a two-player highest-total game, winning the auction always beats losing it by 0.95 regardless of price, so 'always raise' cannot lose and escalation is unbounded.

changes.what: A series of 6 auctions funded from one budget of 100 coins per player. Final score is coins left plus the value of prizes won.
changes.why: Coins spent fighting in one auction are unavailable later, so players must plan across rounds and pick their battles.
changes.fixes: A single one-shot auction gives no planning over several rounds and no budget trade-offs.

changes.what: Each player is secretly dealt their own random order of prize values: the six numbers 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 40, one per auction. Everyone's list totals 140.
changes.why: This is one hidden element. Players must infer from bidding behaviour which auctions rivals value highly. Because every list has the same total, the deal changes what to do, not who is ahead.
changes.fixes: Perfect information: there is no hidden state to infer, only an unbounded test of will.

changes.what: Each auction is played as exactly 3 simultaneous raise stages, with cumulative bids revealed after each stage. All players pay their full cumulative bid (all-pay, as in the original), and the sole highest bidder takes the prize.
changes.why: This keeps the dollar auction's escalation and sunk-cost pressure: after stage 1 you see you are behind and must decide whether to throw more in. The length is fixed and buildable.
changes.fixes: The open-ended alternating raise loop has no fixed number of steps, which the flat step list cannot build cleanly.

changes.what: A tie for the highest cumulative bid leaves the prize unclaimed, though everyone still pays. The winner is whoever has the highest final score.
changes.why: Matching bids is punished rather than rewarded. Restraint (staying out, stopping early) shows up directly in the score, and with three or more players a fighter's loss is the bystander's gain.
changes.fixes: Skill at the game, knowing when to stay out or stop, is not rewarded by a who-ends-higher rule with two players.

changes.what: A simultaneous one-message talk phase before each auction.
changes.why: Players have opposed interests: only one can win, and values are private. Talk enables bluffing about values, proposing bid rings ('you take this one, I take the next'), and testing whether such promises are kept. All of this is non-binding.
changes.fixes: Perfect information: there is no hidden state to infer, only an unbounded test of will.

keeps: Ascending bidding for a prize in which losing bidders also pay what they bid.
The escalation and sunk-cost trap: seeing you are behind, with coins already committed, tempts you to raise past the prize's worth.
Public visibility of the current bids during the auction.
The core lesson that the best move is often not to enter, or to stop early.

recommendation.reason: The escalation trap is a rich strategic idea. It fails only because of the two-player relative-score winner rule and perfect information, and both can be fixed within the limits with more players, a budget across auctions and private prize values.

variation.name: War of Attrition Auctions
variation.summary: Three or four players fight six all-pay auctions from one 100-coin budget. Each auction has three rounds of sealed raises, and every bidder pays what they committed. Each player privately values each prize differently, so escalating against the wrong rival hands the game to whoever stayed out.
variation.rules:
SETUP: Each player starts with 100 coins. Each player is secretly dealt a random ordering of the six prize values 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 40, one value for each of auctions 1 to 6. A player sees only their own list, so every player's six values total 140. Coin totals are public; prize values are private.

The game has 6 auctions (rounds). Each auction proceeds as follows.

1. Announce the auction number.

2. TALK: Every player writes one short message at the same time without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone. Messages are not binding: players may claim values, propose who takes which auction, or bluff.

3. RAISE STAGE 1: At the same time, each player secretly chooses a raise, a whole number from 0 up to their available coins. Available coins are coins held minus everything they have already committed in this auction. Each player's committed bid for this auction becomes the sum of their raises so far. All committed bids are then announced.

4. RAISE STAGE 2: Same as stage 1. Committed bids are announced again.

5. RAISE STAGE 3: Same as stage 1. Final committed bids are announced.

6. RESOLUTION: Every player pays their full committed bid, which is subtracted from their coins, whether or not they win. If exactly one player has the highest committed bid and it is at least 1, that player wins the prize and adds their OWN private value for this auction to their prize points. The value is not revealed to others. If two or more players tie for the highest bid, or all bids are 0, nobody wins the prize.

7. Announce who (if anyone) won and everyone's remaining coins. Committed bids reset to 0 for the next auction.

END: After auction 6, each player's final score is coins remaining plus prize points. All private value lists are then revealed.
variation.objective: The player with the highest final score (coins remaining plus prize points) wins. If two or more players tie for the highest final score, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Simple policies all lose. Never bidding scores exactly 100, which loses to anyone who wins a single prize for less than its value. Going all-in early wins at most one prize worth 40 and finishes with at most 40 points. Any fixed bid can be topped by one coin. Good play means reading which auctions rivals value highly from their stage-1 bids and their talk, then fighting only where your value is high and theirs seems low. It also means cutting losses mid-auction rather than escalating, and remembering that two fighters both lose ground to the bystander. Players disagree on everything: there is one winner, and the values are private. A player who simply follows a proposed rotation ('you take auction 3, I take 4') can be undercut by a rival who breaks the deal on a prize they value at 40, or can give away their own best prize. Talk therefore rewards reading credibility, not just agreeing. Because every value list totals 140, good play rather than the deal decides the winner.

balanced.evidence: Coins and prize points count 1:1. In an auction you win you net v - b; in one you lose you net -b. A bid above your own value can never pay. SEAT/ORDER: all choices and talk are simultaneous polls, so no seat moves first or sees more than another. Every player holds the same multiset {10,15,20,25,30,40}, total 140, so there is no edge from the deal in total. THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (3 players, outcome by the WINNER RULE): (a) ALWAYS PASS gives a fixed score of 100. It draws if both opponents also always pass (100/100/100, no prizes). It loses if any opponent bids 1 into empty auctions: one minimal bidder scores 100 - 6 + 140 = 234. Against two sensible opponents contesting each other, I treat each auction as a two-bidder all-pay contest with values roughly known from talk and bids. The higher-value bidder expects about v_high - v_low. E|v1 - v2| over two independent draws from the value set = 2 x 200 / 36 = 11.1 per auction, so about 67 of rent over 6 auctions, roughly 33 each. Sensible players end near 133 and beat the passer's 100. Always-pass beats only random players, who spend about half their coins in auction 1. That reflects random play being terrible, not the policy being safe against good play. It is not a never-lose policy. (b) ALWAYS ALL-IN AT STAGE 1 pays up to 100 in auction 1 for at most 40, finishes at or below 40 and loses to anyone who passes. (c) ALWAYS BID 1 AT STAGE 1, THEN 0 is overbid by 2 at any later stage, or tied, and loses to any opponent who contests even one auction cheaply. (d) BID 0 UNTIL STAGE 3, THEN SNIPE is just sealed-bid all-pay play and is beaten by opponents who model it. No option is strictly better whatever others do. Bid 0 is beaten by bid 1 when the others pass, and bid 1 is beaten by bid 2. Every player can realistically win, and the payoff labels match the arithmetic: a winner nets v - b and everyone pays their committed bid.

playable.evidence: RULES ARE COMPLETE: raise range, available coins, cumulative commitment, unique-highest test (ties or all-zero bids mean no winner), payment by everyone, scoring and the draw rule are all stated. A player with 0 coins can only raise 0. The game is finite (6 auctions x 3 raise polls) and decided by arithmetic on numbers the game keeps: coins, committed bids and prize points. LIMITS: steps per round. Announce 1. Talk poll 1. Three raise stages at 3 steps each (poll, add raise to committed, announce) = 9. Compute max bid and count ties 1-2. Pay all and conditionally add the private value 1-2: the value is selected by auction number using `if` operations over six value attributes, which is allowed as conditional updates. Announce 1. That is about 15, at most 20. Choice steps: talk plus 3 raises = 4, at most 4. Attributes: 6 values, coins, committed, points, plus a flag = 10, at most 20. Hidden elements 1, at most 3. Random draws per round 0: the deal is a setup shuffle. Rounds 6, at most 40. The unique-highest test uses the player_attribute_compare/calc workaround, which is supported. No board, clock, judge, trade or binding promise is needed. TALK: there are 3-4 players and they genuinely disagree, since each wants the auctions where their own value is high. Following a proposed rotation can cost you, because a designated 1-coin bidder can be sniped at stage 3. Claims about values are something to reason about. Talk is simultaneous, as required. LATE ROUNDS: a bid-1 rotation unravels in auction 6, the one-shot stage-3 snipe. But the safe option (pass, net 0) does not win late rounds. Auction 6 is still a contested sealed all-pay auction where a high private value earns rent, so late play is not trivial.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: CHANCE is limited to how the values line up across players per auction. Every player's six values sum to 140, so in the two-bidder view the sum of (v1 - v2) over the 6 auctions is exactly 0. The positive gaps (A's rent) therefore equal the negative gaps (B's rent), so complete-information equilibrium rents are equal in expectation, about 33 each. With 3-4 players some imbalance from the alignment remains, but it is moderate. I estimate chance at about 25-35% of the result, mainly from alignment and mixed-strategy guessing in sealed stage 3. INFERENCE: values are private and never revealed, even to the winner's opponents. Players must infer them from talk claims, from stage 1-2 commitments (signals versus bluffs), from bids that grow as players chase sunk costs, and from coin totals. They must decide when to concede, since sunk bids are lost anyway, and when to snipe. Spending against a 100-coin budget across six auctions requires planning. When every player plays well, the result is decided by who reads values and opponents' resolve best, not by the deal alone. A deal that lines up high values with others' low values helps, but good play can overcome it because rents are symmetric in expectation. A careless bidder who over-commits or chases sunk bids loses heavily to a disciplined one, so good reasoning is clearly favoured.
